en: The Transmission of the Mind-Dharma Essentials of Chan Master Duanji of Huangbo Mountain.
The Master said to Xiu: "All Buddhas and all sentient beings are but this single mind;
there is no other dharma. Since beginningless time, this mind has never been born and has never ceased. It is neither blue..."
Yellow.
Formless and signless,
it does not belong to existence or non-existence.
It does not reckon between new and old;
it is neither long nor short,
neither large nor small.
Transcending all limits, names, words, traces, and oppositions,
it is the very substance itself;
to stir a thought is immediately to deviate from it.
Just as space is without limit and cannot be measured,
this single mind alone is the Buddha;
there is no further distinction between the Buddha and sentient beings.
However, sentient beings cling to signs and seek externally;
the more they seek, the more they lose,
causing them to seek the Buddha by means of the Buddha.
To seize the mind with the mind,
one could not succeed even throughout kalpas or the remainder of one's life.
One does not realize that when thoughts cease and deliberations are forgotten, the Buddha manifests of itself before one.
This mind is itself the Buddha;
the Buddha is himself sentient beings.
When one is a sentient being, this mind does not diminish.
When one becomes a Buddha, this mind does not increase;
even regarding the myriad practices of the six perfections and merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
these are inherently complete from the beginning and do not require cultivation or augmentation.
When conditions arise, one gives;
when conditions cease, one is tranquil.
If one does not resolutely believe that this is the Buddha, [one will not attain liberation].
Yet to desire to practice by clinging to signs in order to seek spiritual efficacy is entirely delusive thought;
it runs counter to the Way.
This mind is itself the Buddha;
there is no other Buddha,
nor is there any other mind.
This mind is luminously pure,
like space without a single trace of form;
to raise the mind or stir a thought is immediately to deviate from the essence of the Dharma.
This is precisely to be attached to signs.
Since beginningless time, there has been no Buddha who was attached to signs;
rather, one cultivates the six perfections and the myriad practices desiring to attain Buddhahood.
This is precisely the sequence:
since beginningless time, there has been no Buddha who attained enlightenment through a gradual sequence;
rather, one simply awakens to the single mind.
There is not even the slightest dharma to be apprehended;
this is the true Buddha.
The Buddha and sentient beings are of one mind, without distinction.
It is like space, which is neither mixed nor subject to destruction;
it is like the great solar orb illuminating the four continents,
when the sun rises, its light pervades the world.
Space has never been bright;
when the sun sets, darkness pervades the world,
yet space has never been dark.
The realms of light and darkness naturally contend with and supplant one another,
yet the nature of empty space remains vast and unchanging.
The minds of Buddhas and sentient beings are likewise so.
If one contemplates the Buddha as having the marks of pure radiance and liberation,
while contemplating sentient beings as having the marks of defiled turbidity and the darkness of birth-and-death,
one who forms such conceptions will never attain Bodhi, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Because of attachment to signs,
there is nothing whatsoever— no more than a speck of dust— that can be found apart from this single mind;
the mind itself is the Buddha.
Nowadays, those who study the Way do not awaken to the essence of this mind;
instead, they give rise to further thoughts upon the mind itself.
Seeking the Buddha externally and practicing while attached to signs are both evil dharmas.
It is not the path to Bodhi.
To make offerings to all the Buddhas of the ten directions is not as good as making offerings to a single person who has attained the Way beyond the mind.
Why? Because one who is "without mind" is devoid of all minds;
this is the essence of suchness.
Internally, it is like wood or stone—neither moving nor shaking;
externally, it is like empty space—neither obstructed nor hindered.
It is devoid of subject and object, and lacks any spatial location.
It is without characteristics and without gain or loss;
those who would rush toward it dare not enter this Dharma,
for they fear falling into emptiness and finding no place of rest.
Those who withdrew upon seeing the precipice were numerous;
yet, as for those who sought extensively to acquire knowledge and insight,
they were as few as the hairs on a cow’s tail.
The one who realizes the Way is like the horn;
Mañjuśrī represents principle,
while Samantabhadra represents practice.
"Principle" refers to the principle of true emptiness and non-obstruction;
"practice" refers to the inexhaustible practice of detachment from signs.
Avalokiteśvara embodies great compassion.
Śrī-garbha (Shi-zhi) shall be the Great Wisdom.
Vimalakīrti means "Pure Name.
"Pure" refers to the nature.
A name is a characteristic.
Since nature and characteristics are not different,
he is titled "Pure Name" (Vimalakīrti).
That which is represented by all the great Bodhisattvas exists within every person;
it is precisely this that one realizes by not departing from the single mind.
This is the case for those who study the Way today.
To not realize [the truth] within one's own mind,
but instead to grasp at objects by clinging to appearances outside the mind,
is to turn one's back on the Way.
Regarding the sands of the Ganges,
the Buddha said they are but sand;
yet the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śakras, Brahmās, and all the devas tread upon them as they pass by.
The sand does not rejoice when it is trodden upon by cattle, sheep, insects, or ants;
nor does the sand feel anger.
The sand is neither greedy for rare treasures and fragrant scents,
nor does it loathe excrement, urine, and foul odors;
this mind is the mind that is no-mind.
Free from all marks,
there is no further distinction between sentient beings and all Buddhas;
it is simply a matter of being able to be without mind.
This is the ultimate realization.
If a student of the Way does not directly attain a state of no-mind,
they will never achieve the Way, even if they practice for kalpas on end.
They are bound by the practices and deeds of the three vehicles and cannot attain liberation.
Nevertheless, there is variation in the speed with which one realizes this mind;
there are those who, upon hearing the Dharma for a single thought-moment, immediately attain the state of no-mind.
There are those who attain the state of no-mind upon reaching the ten levels of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, or the ten transferences; once they have attained no-mind,
whether through long or short practice, they abide therein,
with nothing further to cultivate or realize.
In truth, there is nothing to be attained;
it is real and not false,
realized in a single thought-moment.
Those who attain it through the ten stages expend their efforts in vain and undergo needless toil;
this is not at all equal to recognizing the fundamental Dharma for oneself directly upon hearing the words.
This dharma is precisely the mind;
there is no dharma apart from the mind.
This mind is precisely the dharma.
Outside of phenomena there is no mind;
the mind itself is mindless,
and there is not even one who is mindless.
To intend for the mind to be without mind is,
on the contrary, to make the mind have something;
it is simply a matter of silent resonance.
It transcends all conceptualization;
therefore, it is said that "the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
This mind is the Buddha of primordial purity.
All beings possess this.
Even the wriggling and crawling creatures that harbor life are of one essence with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, no different at all.
It is only because of deluded thoughts and discrimination that they create various karmic fruits.
In the ultimate reality of the primordial Buddha, there is not a single thing;
it is merely empty penetration,
quiescence, clarity, wondrousness, and peace.
One awakens and enters deeply by oneself;
it is right here and now.
Perfectly complete and fully endowed, there is nothing further lacking.
Even if one practices with diligence throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and traverses all the stages,
or even at the moment of realization in a single thought,
one realizes only that one was originally and inherently a Buddha.
Above this, not even a single thing can be added;
yet when one observes the efforts exerted throughout kalpas,
they are all merely deluded actions within a dream.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said:
"In regard to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I have truly nothing to obtain.
If there were anything to obtain..."
Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon me.
Furthermore, it is said:
"This Dharma is equal."
There is neither high nor low;
this is called bodhi.
It is precisely this original source, the pure mind.
Together with all sentient beings, the worlds of the Buddhas, and the mountains and rivers,
whether possessing form or being formless, they pervade the realms of the ten directions;
all are equal, without the marks of "self" or "other."
This fundamental source, the pure mind,
is eternally self-perfect, luminous, and all-illuminating;
yet worldly people do not awaken to it.
One merely identifies seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing as the mind,
and is thus shrouded by these very functions; for this reason,
one does not perceive the essence of the luminous spirit.
Simply by being directly without mind,
the fundamental essence manifests of itself;
it is like the great sun-disk rising in the void, illuminating the ten directions everywhere without further obstruction.
Therefore, practitioners of the Way merely recognize seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, as well as purposeful activity and movement.
If one empties out seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,
the path of the mind is cut off and there is no place for entry.
One merely recognizes the fundamental mind within the spheres of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;
yet the fundamental mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing,
and knowing, nor is it separate from them.
Do not give rise to views or interpretations based on what is seen, heard, sensed, or known.
Do not stir thoughts regarding what is seen, heard, sensed, or known.
Nor should you seek the mind apart from what is seen, heard, sensed, or known.
Furthermore, do not abandon seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to grasp at dharmas;
neither identify with them nor distance yourself from them;
do not dwell in them and do not cling to them.
Moving freely and acting with mastery in all directions, there is nothing that is not a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
When people of the world hear of the Way,
they say that all Buddhas transmit the Dharma of the Mind.
They assume that there is a separate dharma apart from the mind that can be realized or grasped;
they consequently seek the dharma by means of the mind,
not realizing that the mind itself is the dharma and the dharma itself is the mind.
One must not seek the mind further within the mind;
even after passing through ten million kalpas, there will never be a day of attainment.
It is better to be without-mind right now.
This is precisely the Original Dharma.
It is like a strong man who, having lost the jewel within his own forehead, goes outward in search of it;
though he travels throughout the ten directions, he will ultimately never find it.
When the wise point this out, one sees for oneself that the original pearl is as it was before.
Thus, practitioners of the Way are deluded regarding their own fundamental mind and do not recognize it as Buddha;
consequently, they seek outwardly, giving rise to practices of effortful cultivation.
To realize [the Way] through successive stages,
seeking it diligently throughout kalpas without ever attaining it,
is not as good as being mindless in the present moment.
One definitively knows that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent and unobtainable;
they are without support and without abiding.
Without capacity and without object,
by not moving from deluded thought one realizes bodhi.
At the moment of realizing the Way, one realizes nothing other than the Buddha of one's own original mind.
The efforts expended over kalpas are all in vain;
it is like a strongman who, upon finding his jewel,
finds only the one originally on his forehead.
It does not depend on the power of seeking outwardly;
therefore, the Buddha said:
"In regard to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I have truly attained nothing."
Fearing that people might not believe this, I cite what is seen by the five eyes and what is spoken by the five modes of speech;
it is true and not false, for this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Practitioners of the Way should not doubt that the four great elements constitute the body.
The four great elements are without self,
and the self likewise has no master;
therefore, one should know that this body is without self and without master.
The five aggregates constitute the mind.
Since the five aggregates are without self and without a master,
one should know that this mind is likewise without self and without a master.
The arising and ceasing of the conjunction of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses is likewise thus.
Since the eighteen elements are empty,
all things are entirely empty.
Only the fundamental mind remains vast and pure.
There is the food of consciousness and the food of wisdom;
yet the body of the four elements suffers from the affliction of the ulcer of hunger.
To provide sustenance in accordance with need without giving rise to greedy attachment is called "food of wisdom.
To indulge one's desires in seeking flavors and give rise to false discrimination is not.
Seeking only that which suits the palate without giving rise to revulsion or detachment—
this is called the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).
This refers to the Śrāvakas.
Because they attain enlightenment by means of sound,
they are called Śrāvakas; however,
they do not understand their own minds.
One gives rise to understanding through the oral teachings,
or perhaps through supernormal powers,
or through auspicious signs.
Regarding the activity of speech:
it is heard that there are those who cultivate the path to Buddhahood over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* for the sake of Bodhi and Nirvana;
these all belong to the path of the Śrāvakas.
This is called the Buddha of the Śrāvaka:
one who directly and suddenly realizes that one's own mind is fundamentally the Buddha.
There is not a single dharma to be attained;
there is not a single practice to be cultivated.
This is the unsurpassed path.
This is the Buddha of True Suchness.
A student of the Way only fears that for even a single thought there is existence.
One is then separated from the Way.
To have every thought-moment free of marks and every thought-moment free of conditioned action is itself the Buddha.
If a practitioner of the Way wishes to attain Buddhahood,
they need not study all the Buddha-dharmas collectively;
they should only study non-seeking and non-attachment.
When there is no seeking, the mind does not arise;
when there is no attachment, the mind does not cease.
This non-arising and non-ceasing is itself the Buddha.
The eighty-four thousand Dharma gates correspond to the eighty-four thousand afflictions;
they are merely gates for teaching and guiding others.
Fundamentally, there are no dharmas at all.
Detachment is itself the Dharma;
he who knows detachment is a Buddha.
It is simply the relinquishing of all afflictions.
This is a dharma that cannot be apprehended.
If a practitioner of the Way wishes to know the essential secret,
they need only ensure that not a single thing is attached to the mind.
To say that the Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space means that this is a metaphor for the Dharma-body being identical to empty space,
and empty space being identical to the Dharma-body.
Ordinary people say that the Dharma-body pervades all places within empty space,
and that empty space contains the Dharma-body;
they do not realize that the Dharma-body is itself empty space and empty space is itself the Dharma-body.
If one definitively asserts that space exists,
then space is not the Dharma-body;
if one definitively asserts that the Dharma-body exists, [then it is not space].
The Dharma-body is not empty space,
yet do not interpret it as being empty space;
empty space itself is the Dharma-body.
Do not form the interpretation that it is the Dharma-body;
the Dharma-body is itself space.
Space and the Dharma-body have no distinguishing characteristics.
The Buddha and sentient beings have no distinguishing characteristics;
birth-and-death and nirvana have no distinguishing characteristics;
afflictions and bodhi have no distinguishing characteristics.
To be free from all marks is itself the Buddha.
Ordinary people grasp at objects;
practitioners of the Way grasp at the mind.
The simultaneous forgetting of both mind and objects is the true Dharma.
Forgetting objects is still relatively easy; forgetting the mind is extremely difficult.
People do not dare to forget their own minds.
Fearing one might fall into a void where there is nothing to grasp,
one fails to realize that emptiness is fundamentally not empty;
it is solely the True Dharma-realm.
This nature of numinous awareness has, since beginningless time, coexisted with empty space;
it has never been born and never ceased,
never having existed and never having been non-existent.
Never defiled, never pure;
never clamorous, never tranquil;
never young, never old.
It has no location and no interior or exterior;
it has no quantity and no form;
it has no color or image and no sound.
It cannot be sought, it cannot be pursued;
it cannot be cognized by wisdom,
nor can it be grasped through words.
It cannot be realized through objects and phenomena;
it cannot be attained through effort.
This applies equally to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as well as to all sentient beings, down to the smallest crawling insects.
This very nature of Great Nirvāṇa is the nature;
this nature is the mind;
and the mind is the Buddha.
The Buddha is itself the Dharma.
A single thought that departs from truth is entirely delusion;
one must not seek the mind further by means of the mind.
One cannot seek the Buddha further through the Buddha,
nor can one seek the Dharma further through the Dharma. Therefore,
the practitioner of the Way simply attains silent resonance with the mind directly beneath them.
To conceive a thought is already a deviation.
To transmit mind by means of mind is the correct view.
Be careful not to pursue external objects.
To mistake the objective realm for the mind is like mistaking a thief for one's own son;
because of the presence of greed, anger, and delusion, one establishes the precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Since there is fundamentally no affliction, how could there be bodhi?
Thus the Patriarch said:
"The Buddha taught all dharmas."
To eliminate all mental states,
I have no mental states at all;
what use have I for all dharmas?
Above the Buddha of Primordial Purity,
not even a single thing can be attached;
it is like empty space which, though adorned with immeasurable precious jewels, can never be made to abide therein.
The Buddha-nature is identical to empty space;
although it is adorned with immeasurable merit and wisdom, it can never be made to abide [in any specific state].
It is merely that, being deluded regarding its own nature, one fails to see it.
This is what is called the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground.
All phenomena are established in dependence upon this mind;
they exist when encountering objects and cease to exist when there are no objects.
One must not transform the nature of purity into an object of cognition.
What are called concentration and wisdom are the vivid functions of clear discernment.
To perceive stillness and alertness through seeing, hearing,
sensing, and knowing is entirely to form interpretations based on objects;
this may suffice for those of middling or inferior faculties when explained temporarily.
If one wishes to realize this through direct personal experience, one must not form such views.
All these are merely objective phenomena that have either emerged from or dissolved back into the realm of existence (*bhava*).
One should simply refrain from forming views of existence or non-existence regarding all phenomena.
This is precisely the realization of the Dharma.
On the first day of the ninth month, the Master said to Xiu:
"Since Master Bodhidharma arrived in China..."
I teach only the single mind and transmit only the single Dharma.
Since it is from Buddha to Buddha, I do not speak of other Buddhas;
since it is from Dharma to Dharma, I do not speak of other Dharmas.
The Dharma is the ineffable Dharma;
the Buddha is the ungraspable Buddha;
this is precisely the fundamentally pure mind of the source.
This alone is the one true reality;
the other two are not real.
Prajñā is wisdom.
This wisdom is precisely the fundamental mind of signlessness.
Ordinary beings do not pursue the Way;
they merely indulge their six sense-faculties and thus wander through the six realms of existence.
When a practitioner of the Way calculates birth and death in a single thought-moment, they immediately fall into the path of Māra.
When a single thought-moment gives rise to various views, they immediately fall into the path of externalists.
To perceive that there is a realm of birth and its subsequent extinction—[is the error].
One then falls into the path of the śrāvaka;
seeing neither arising nor anything but cessation,
one falls into the path of the pratyekabuddha.
Phenomena are fundamentally unborn and now likewise unextinguished.
One does not give rise to dualistic views, neither loathing nor rejoicing.
All phenomena are but this single mind.
Only then does one attain the Buddha-vehicle.
Ordinary people all give rise to thoughts by pursuing external objects;
their minds consequently experience longing and aversion.
If one wishes for there to be no objects, one should forget the mind.
When the mind is forgotten, objects become empty;
when objects are empty, the mind ceases.
If one does not forget the mind but merely attempts to eliminate objects,
the objects cannot be eliminated;
it will only serve to increase confusion and turmoil.
Therefore, all phenomena are mind-only;
yet even the mind cannot be apprehended.
What more, then, is there to seek?
One who studies Prajñā does not perceive that there is a single dharma to be attained;
they sever their intent toward the three vehicles,
for there is only the one true reality.
It cannot be realized.
To think, "I can realize it" or "I can attain it," is the mark of one who possesses overweening pride.
Those who cast off their robes and departed during the assembly at the Lotus Sutra were all members of this class.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
Regarding Bodhi, I have truly attained nothing; it is merely a matter of silent resonance.
When an ordinary person is about to die, they should simply contemplate that the five aggregates are all empty and the four elements are without self.
The true mind is without marks; it neither departs nor arrives.
At the time of birth, its nature does not come;
at the time of death, its nature does not go.
Tranquil and perfectly quiescent, the mind and its objects are as one.
If you can simply be thus,
you will directly and suddenly realize it.
To be unbound by the three periods of time is to be a person who has transcended the world.
One must not have even the slightest inclination or pursuit.
If one sees auspicious signs, such as the Buddhas coming to welcome them and various manifestations appearing before them,
one should not have the mind follow them away.
If one sees inauspicious signs, various [unfavorable] things manifesting before one, [one should likewise remain unmoved].
Furthermore, there is no fear in the mind;
rather, one simply forgets the mind,
becoming identical with the dharma-realm.
One will then attain mastery;
this is the essential point.
On the eighth day of the tenth month.
The Master said to Xiu:
"As for what is called the 'transformed city,' it refers to the two vehicles, as well as the ten stages, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment."
All of these are provisional teachings established for the purpose of guiding and attracting beings;
they are all merely "transformed cities" (pariṇāmanī-nagara).
As for what is called the "Jewel Place" (ratnasthāna), [it refers to the ultimate goal].
This is the treasure of the self-nature of the true mind’s original Buddha.
This treasure does not belong to the realm of emotional or intellectual measurement;
it cannot be established through conceptual construction.
There is no Buddha and no sentient beings;
there is no agent and no object.
Where, then, could a city exist?
If it is asked, "Since this is already a conjured city,
where is the treasure trove?
the treasure trove cannot be pointed out.
The finger merely has a location;
it is not the locus of the true treasure.
Therefore, it is said that [the treasure] is simply near.
It cannot be defined by fixed measures;
one should simply realize and accord with it as it is.
As for the term "icchantika":
They lack faith.
All sentient beings in the six realms of existence, even those of the two vehicles, who do not believe in the fruit of Buddhahood,
are all termed icchantikas who have severed their roots of goodness.
A bodhisattva has deep faith in the existence of the Buddha-dharma and does not perceive the distinction between the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.
The Buddha and sentient beings share the same dharma-nature;
this is what is called the "icchantika of roots of goodness.
Generally speaking, those who attain awakening through the teachings of sound [the scriptures] are [of this type].
Those who are called Śrāvakas are those who awaken by contemplating causes and conditions; those who are called Pratyekabuddhas are likewise those who awaken by contemplating causes and conditions.
If one does not awaken within one's own mind,
even if one attains Buddhahood,
it is still called the Buddhahood of a Śrāvaka.
Those who study the Way mostly attain awakening through the teachings and doctrines,
rather than through the mind-nature itself; thus,
even though they practice for kalpas, [they do not realize it].
In the end, this is not the fundamental Buddha.
If one does not awaken within the mind,
one must at least awaken within the teachings.
Thus, one treats the mind lightly while valuing the teachings,
eventually becoming like a dog chasing a clod of earth while forgetting its own nature; therefore,
simply accord with the fundamental mind and there is no need to seek the Dharma.
The mind is itself the Dharma.
Generally, ordinary people are often obstructed by objects in their minds and hindered by phenomena in their principles.
One constantly desires to escape from sensory objects in order to settle the mind,
and to withdraw from affairs in order to preserve principle;
yet one does not realize that this is actually the mind obstructing objects and principle obstructing affairs.
Simply let the mind be empty and the objects will naturally be empty;
simply let the principle be tranquil and the phenomena will naturally be tranquil.
Do not apply the mind in a perverted manner.
Ordinary people for the most part are unwilling to embrace emptiness,
fearing they will fall into nihilism;
they do not realize that their own minds are fundamentally empty.
The foolish eliminate external phenomena but do not eliminate the mind;
the wise eliminate the mind but do not eliminate external phenomena.
The Bodhisattva’s mind is like space.
One relinquishes everything;
all the merit one has performed is not grasped with attachment.
Furthermore, there are three grades of such relinquishment.
One completely relinquishes all internal and external body and mind,
remaining like empty space without any grasping or attachment;
thereafter, one responds to things according to their circumstances.
When both subject and object are forgotten,
this is called great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
If one practices the path and spreads virtue on only one side, [it is not so].
To relinquish while simultaneously being free from any expectation of reward is what constitutes intermediate equanimity.
If one extensively cultivates various virtues with expectations,
yet upon hearing the Dharma realizes emptiness and consequently becomes unattached.
This is called minor relinquishment.
Great relinquishment is like a torch held before one;
there is no further delusion or awakening.
Intermediate equanimity is like a candle held beside one;
it may be bright or dim.
Minor equanimity is like a candle held behind one.
Because they do not perceive pits or traps,
the bodhisattva’s mind is like space,
relinquishing everything.
The past mind is unattainable;
this is the relinquishing of the past.
The present mind is unattainable.
This is present relinquishment.
A future mind is unattainable;
this is future relinquishment.
This refers to the simultaneous relinquishment of the three periods of time.
Ever since the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma to Kāśyapa,
it has been transmitted from mind to mind by means of the seal of the mind.
Mind and mind are not different.
If a seal is applied to emptiness, the seal does not form a character;
if a seal is applied to a material object, the seal does not form a dharma.
Therefore, one uses the mind to seal the mind;
mind and mind are not different.
Yet, that which can seal and that which is sealed are both difficult to bring into accord.
Therefore, those who attain it are few.
Yet, the mind is itself no-mind;
attainment is itself non-attainment.
The Buddha has three bodies.
The Dharma-body (dharmakāya) teaches the self-nature of phenomena as empty and pervasive;
the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) teaches all pure phenomena.
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) preaches the Dharma of the six perfections and myriad practices;
the dharma-body (dharmakāya) preaches the Dharma,
which cannot be sought through speech, sound, physical form, or written characters.
There is nothing to be taught and nothing to be realized;
it is simply the spontaneous penetration of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, it is said:
That which cannot be spoken of as a dharma is what is called the teaching of the Dharma.
The Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) and the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) both manifest according to the perceptions and conditions of sentient beings;
the teachings they expound likewise respond to specific circumstances and accord with the faculties of beings in order to gather and transform them.
None of these are the true Dharma.
Therefore it is said:
"The retributive and transformation bodies are not the true Buddha."
Nor is it the one who preaches the Dharma.
What is spoken of as "the same single brilliant spirit divided into six harmonious combinations"—
this "single brilliant spirit" refers to:
"One mind" refers to the sixth [consciousness].
"The six harmonious unions" refers to the six sense faculties.
These six sense faculties each conjoin with their respective objects:
the eye conjoins with form;
the ear conjoins with sound.
The nose is conjoined with odors;
the tongue is conjoined with flavors;
the body is conjoined with tangibles.
When the mind and mental objects come together,
the six consciousnesses arise in between, forming the eighteen realms.
If one realizes that these eighteen realms are non-existent, [one attains liberation].
The six harmonious aggregates are bound together into a single refined spirit;
this single refined spirit is precisely the mind.
Those who study the Way all know this;
yet they cannot avoid interpreting it as a single, brilliant intelligence joined with the six elements.
